title: Nachiketa at Death's door
hookLine: a boy waits three days at Death's house and asks what happens after

lines: TO WHOM WILL YOU GIVE ME?
cards: To whom will you give me? A boy asks his father that in the middle of a great sacrifice, where the father is giving away what he owns, including cows too old to give milk. The boy asks a second time.
Then a third. And the father, losing patience, snaps: to Death I give you. That's how the Katha Upanishad, a Hindu scripture, begins.

teach.b: First, the waiting. Nachiketa reaches the house of Yama, lord of death, and Yama is away. The boy waits three nights without food.
When Yama comes home he is troubled, because a guest has gone unfed in his house, and he offers three wishes, one for each night. Second, the question.
Nachiketa spends his first wish on his father, that he'll be calm and glad to see him again. The second is to learn a sacred fire.

teach.h: DO THEY STILL EXIST, OR NOT?
teach.b: The third is the question itself: when someone dies, some say they still are, and some say they are not. Teach me which. Third, the refusal.
Yama tries to wriggle out of it. Even the gods have doubted about this, he says; it's subtle; ask for something else.
He lays out the alternatives: sons and grandsons, cattle and gold, horses, land, a long life, chariots and music. Nachiketa turns them all down. These things wear out, he says.
Keep your horses, keep your songs. I want the answer.
Fourth, the good and the pleasant.
Only now does Yama begin to teach. Two things come to a person, he says: the good and the pleasant. The wise choose the good.
What follows is his teaching on the self that is not born and does not die.
Hindus read this Upanishad as scripture, and teachers keep coming back to Nachiketa: a boy at Death's door who would rather have a true answer than everything Death can give him.

how: Hindus study the Katha Upanishad as scripture, often with a teacher, and the story of Nachiketa is told to children and adults as a teaching on courage, truth and the self.

o: a Hindu sage who gave away cows too old for milk
the boy who waits at Death's house to ask what follows death
the lord of death who offers a boy three wishes

games.q: the boy at Death's door — tap the pairs.
p: the boy who waits and asks

s: Nachiketa goes to Death's house out of curiosity
his father's angry words send him: to Death I give you.
Yama says even the gods have doubted about this question
he says it's subtle, and asks the boy to choose another wish.
Nachiketa's first wish is the question about death
his first wish is for his father; the question is his third.

games.q: you're Nachiketa. Death offers you a long life, gold, horses and music, if you'll just drop your question. what do you do?
o: take the gold and the long life.
refuse it all and keep the question.
games.why: he turns everything down: these things wear out, keep your horses and songs. only then does Yama teach him.

practice: Let your biggest question come up, not the one you'd put on a form but the one underneath: about death, or a person, or what any of this is for. Say it to yourself in one plain sentence, and don't try to answer it.
Just hold it, the way Nachiketa held his through three hungry nights, and if other thoughts crowd in, come back to the sentence.

wordCard.voice: Nachiketa, the boy in the Katha Upanishad who waits at Yama's house and asks what happens after death. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: shreyas, the good, which Yama sets beside preyas, the pleasant (Katha Upanishad 1.2).

carryVoice: Your line: Nachiketa's question. He wanted the answer more than the horses. Day seven hundred seventy-one.
